title: There are no Collatz m-cycles with m ≤ 91
notes: Journal of Integer Sequences 26 (2023) Article 23.3.5. Proves every nontrivial Collatz m-cycle has m≥92, where m is the number of local minima. Valley arrangement carries cycle information beyond (K,L) parity counts; the argument is Diophantine, not spectral. Cited from docs/problems/juggler_cycle_word_functional.md. READ FROM THE PDF, 19 September 2026 (docs/problems/juggler_collatz_finance_mirror.md): Definition 4 takes the floor X_0 = 695 * 2^60; the introduction attributes the period bound K > 7.2e10 odd steps to Hercher and Puchert 2018 (hercher-2018-collatz-cycle-length); Lemma 8 is the 2-adic run congruence, k consecutive odd steps force n = -1 mod 2^k hence n >= 2^k - 1; Theorem 16 is the finance identity 2^(K+L) = product over odd n of (3 + 1/n) with T(n_i) the reciprocal sum over a run; Corollary 17 gives sum T(n_i) <= (97/54) m/X_0; Theorem 27 gives sum T(n_i) <= (3/4) K/X_0 independently of m via Lemma 26's averaging over at most three consecutive runs; Corollary 29 reaches X_0 >= 1536 * 2^60 by tracking residue classes modulo powers of two computationally. CORRECTION to the earlier sentence 'the Juggler run-type count e is the analogous valley count': Paper A's Theorem 3.31 bounds the number of even letters by a census of run forms, while Hercher bounds the number of local minima by a Diophantine argument; the Juggler m-cycle problem is open for every m, including m = 1 (J-cycle-gaps-are-mirror-images, J-collatz-walk-charge-constant). THE FINAL SECTION, placed 20 September 2026: it proves that to raise the odd-step count of a nontrivial cycle to the next bound, K >= 1.375 * 10^11, it suffices to verify convergence for every integer up to 1536 * 2^60 = 3 * 2^69 (Corollary 29, residue classes tracked modulo powers of two), nearly 60 percent less range than the finance-type bounds need; the abstract states 'Simons and de Weger proved m >= 76', 'with newer bounds ... m >= 83', and the paper's m >= 92. Barina 2025 (barina-2025-collatz-verification-limit) verified through 2^71 = 2048 * 2^60 and states the consequence, citing this paper: the length of a nontrivial cycle rises to 355504839929 in the standard count, i.e. 217976794617 shortcut steps with 137528045312 odd ones, the second survivor of Paper A's Theorem 5.18 at 2^71; the finance alone would keep the first survivor, 114208327604, until 2^71.88. Paper A's Theorem 5.18 records this since the 20 September evening edition. Whether m rises above 91 at 2^71 would need this paper's Diophantine analysis redone at the new floor; not done here. READ AT THEOREM 27, LEMMA 26 AND COROLLARY 29 from the arXiv PDF (2201.00406), 21 September 2026, local copy under literature/sources/. LEMMA 26 is the averaging: for one, two or three consecutive runs, sum T(n_i) < (sum k_i) * (3/4) * (1/X_0), by a case analysis on k_i in {1, 2, 3, >=4} and l_i, using that k_i consecutive odd steps force n_i = -1 mod 2^(k_i). THEOREM 27 is its m-free consequence, delta < (K+L)/K < delta + (1/(3 log 2)) * (3/4) * (1/X_0) with K the odd count, which in the linear form reads Lambda < (1/4) * K_odd / X_0. COROLLARY 29 is the residue tracking: a C++ run over the Lemma 26 cases tracks n_i modulo powers of two and drops any case whose class has its least positive member above the needed bound, so a verified floor of 1536 * 2^60 does the work of 3781 * 2^60; five weeks on eight cores. NEITHER TRANSPOSES USEFULLY TO 3n-1, measured the same day (tests/research/juggler_sequence/test_negative_m_cycles.py::test_one_of_herchers_refinements_would_now_reach_and_the_other_still_does_not). Corollary 29's gain is a factor 2.46, 1.30 bits; closing the first open value of Paper D, m = 59 at the floor 2^51, needs 4.18 bits, and m = 60 to 63 need 4.20 to 4.27. Theorem 27's constant, 0.1577 per unit of total cycle length, is 0.23 bits tighter than the laboratory's own 0.1845, which is kernel-checked (neg_cycle_finance), but the m-free period bound is unchanged at 85137581 under it, because the surviving lengths are near-convergents of log2/log3 and a seventeen per cent change of the window removes none of them. WHAT REMAINS WORTH TRANSPOSING is the valley arrangement behind his Main Theorem 21, a different mechanism from either of these; Lemma 8 itself is already the note's Lemma 1. AMENDED LATER THE SAME DAY, AFTER PAPER D 1.1.0. The shortfalls quoted above were measured against Paper D 1.0.0's bound. Version 1.1.0 adds the valley count, which is this paper's Main Theorem 21 arrangement transposed, and moves the first open value from m = 59 to m = 62; remeasured against the refined bound, closing m = 62 needs 0.30 bits of effective floor, m = 63 needs 0.62 and m = 64 needs 1.99, against Corollary 29's 1.30. So Corollary 29 would now close two further values of m and fall short at the third, and it is no longer a method wall; it is reclassified OPEN, WORTH TRYING. Nothing measured shows the residue argument carries to a map whose odd step subtracts, and Lemma 26's cases have no negative-side statement yet, so this is a reason to attempt the transposition rather than a result. Theorem 27's verdict is unchanged. THE VALLEY ARRANGEMENT IS TRANSPOSED: it is Lemma 6 of Paper D 1.1.0, proved through a threshold rather than a vertex enumeration, and run on this paper's own side at its floor 695 * 2^60 the six lemmas give m <= 90 against its published 91. COROLLARY 29 ATTEMPTED AND MEASURED, 21 September 2026, same day, after the reclassification above. Both halves transpose. Lemma 26's case analysis has an exact negative-side statement: the note's Lemma 1 makes the run exact, so a run from the local minimum y with u = y - 1 and a = v_2(u) contributes T(y) < kappa(a)/u with kappa(a) = 1 - (2/3)^a, the same factor Remark 7 carries as 3(1 - (2/3)^k)/n, and the relation between consecutive minima is u_i = (2/3)^(a_i) (2^(r_i)(u_(i+1)+1) - 1) against his n_i = (2/3)^(k_i)(2^(l_i) n_(i+1) + 1) - 1, the same shape sign-flipped, so the one/two/three-run averaging carries case for case with the same rationals (1/4 at a=1, 5/8 at a=2, 19/27 at a=3). The residue drop is available and sharper: Lemma 1 is the run congruence, Lemma 5 makes each case word a residue class, and since every minimum of a window is above the floor the drop uses the least member of the class above the floor, not the least positive member. WHAT FAILS IS THE SIZE, BECAUSE IT IS A DIFFERENT CONSTANT'S SIZE. Corollary 29 improves Theorem 27's m-free constant; Paper D's open values turn on Lemma 6's valley cap, not on any m-free bound (at m = 62 the chaining display clears by 41.4 bits). The cap is minimised with four minima at the floor at m = 62 and five at m = 63, and an averaging argument can act on nothing else. Measured at 2^51 against version 1.1.0's bound: m = 62 needs those four to average 0.8137 and four consecutive minima above 2^51 attain 0.9013 (start 2255557997555713, runs 12, 7, 5, 6); m = 63 needs five to average 0.6509 and five attain 0.8689 (start 2266848965985921, runs 7, 5, 7, 5, 6). So the refinement is worth at most 0.150 bits of the 0.297 m = 62 needs and 0.203 of the 0.619 m = 63 needs, charging it no boundary loss at all. A single minimum gives nothing (2^51 + 1 has kappa within 1e-9 of one); eight consecutive average 0.719, so the gain grows with the block, and the block grows with m and with the floor: at 2^60 the row m = 76 demands 0.7535 against an attained 0.7579, short by 0.008 bits. RECLASSIFIED METHOD WALL AGAIN, for a structural reason rather than a size one. Implementation and witnesses: src/research/juggler_sequence/negative_valley_windows.py, pinned by tests/research/juggler_sequence/test_negative_m_cycles.py (three tests; the known-bad input is a one per cent strengthening of kappa, which excludes both real cycles at their own least element).
